prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part for optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. After the first round I have tested the case against the chair's questions, and the core still holds. The discovery is a specific idea, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels on the clock transition, which opened a regime that neither the frequency comb nor single-ion clocks contain: thousands of atoms interrogated at once, with stability and systematic control that reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. That changed what the field can do, and it is now doing physics, through centimetre-scale redshift measurements and bounds on variation of constants. It has been confirmed by several independent laboratories whose clocks agree at that level, and roughly two decades of development separate the proposal from today, so nobody can call it premature. Attribution is the cleanest of the three leading ballots, because the concept and first demonstration (Katori) and the accuracy and systematic-control record (Ye) map onto two names with no one visibly excluded from the credited list. On the chair's maturity question, this is the candidate where the established core and the whole credited claim are the same thing, which is why I weigh it as I do. I do not propose it because a pending redefinition of the second makes it fashionable; the redefinition is a consequence of the science and should not decide the prize either way.
statement.case_against: I have to take the novelty objection more seriously after reading the round-1 exchange, because Eriksson, Olsson, Mehlig, Danielsson and the chair all raise it from different sides. The prizes of 2005 and 2012 sit close, and a committee that wants to reward discovery of new matter may reasonably weigh topological insulators or moire materials above a gain in measurement precision. I think the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept, but I accept that this is a judgement of weighting that reasonable members can make differently. Second, my support is narrow: with four members preferring B025 and two B013, I cannot claim a consensus, and my familiarity with the laser-spectroscopy side may make me overrate it. Third, credit among clock groups (PTB, SYRTE, Tokyo, JILA) is wider than two names, and the citation has to be written so that it does not claim the whole of optical clocks or lean on comb and ion-clock technology.

responses.point: Johansson argues that B025 is not premature because the phenomena (correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity at the magic angle) are widely reproduced, and that the open question is theoretical (pairing), not experimental, so the timing objection should carry less weight.
responses.response: That is a fair correction of my opening ranking. If there were conflicting experimental results I would hold to my timing worry, and there are not: the phenomenon is reproduced. I therefore no longer rest my case on the claim that twisted graphene is premature, and I rank B025 as a real alternative. What remains for me is attribution, not timing. The three-name set leaves out Andrei, whose flat-band and van Hove evidence you yourself describe as a genuine experimental contribution, and you have asked for a citation that does not imply nobody saw flat-band signatures before 2018. That is a worse position than the Katori-Ye pair, where no one with a comparable documented claim is left outside the credited list. So we may agree on the science of B025 and still weigh the credit problem differently.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B006 with the same two names but says the citation should not lean on comb technology, would resist adding platform names, and would not make the prize hinge on the undecided redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on all three points and I am adopting them in the final wording. The citation is now tied to the lattice-clock concept and the many-atom regime, and it does not mention combs or ion clocks. I also withdraw the weight I gave the redefinition of the second in my first statement: it is a downstream consequence and the committee has not been given a decision date, so it should not count for or against the prize. Where I would press you slightly is your concession in round 1 that a Katori-Ye prize could be accused of drawing a line through a communal achievement. I think the answer is the one you gave: the proposer and the group that delivered the record are the natural pair, and I would resist adding Takamoto, Ludlow or Lemke because the credited list is two names.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B006 only as an alternative because the physics originality is smaller: it refines well-understood atomic transitions and builds on the comb and ion-clock prizes, whereas twisted bilayer graphene revealed a previously unknown regime of correlated electrons.
responses.response: I accept the distinction you draw between a discovery of new matter and a metrological achievement, and I think the committee should state it openly. I disagree that the lattice clock merely refines a known regime. The comb counts optical cycles and the ion clock gives a quantum-logic route with a single absorber; neither contains the magic-wavelength condition or the many-atom regime, and the many-atom regime brings its own physics, namely collisional and lattice-site interaction shifts that had to be understood before 1e-18 was reachable. The relevant measure for me is what the work changed about what can be measured, and the clock changed it by orders of magnitude. If the committee's rule is that matter discovery outranks measurement, I will say so is a coherent rule, but the rule should then be applied to the other candidates in the same way, as Johansson and Lindroth ask.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with a citation confined to the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 idea, and argues that the overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases is limited.
responses.response: Your argument on the 2016 overlap persuades me that novelty is not the main problem for B013: time-reversal-protected Z2 insulators and their HgTe realisation are a different class from the bulk topological invariant honoured in 2016, and I withdraw the overlap concern from my own list of reasons. My remaining difficulty is the one the chair's questions highlight, that the credit is compound. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state that Molenkamp measured, and Hasan's three-dimensional work is a separate discovery; Danielsson and you both say the citation must stay with the two-dimensional effect, which is the honest course. Given that, I rank B013 as my first alternative and I would be content with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp if the committee decided against clocks, because the trio is the best that can be done from the available names.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that prediction followed by discovery is the cleaner structure and that B025 maps one prediction and one experiment onto three names, while B013 forces an arbitrary cut through a compound credit.
responses.response: I agree that prediction followed by confirmation is the cleaner structure, and I think B006 has it too, with Katori's magic-wavelength proposal first and the strontium demonstration after it. I would add, though, that B025 does not map as neatly onto three names as you suggest, since you yourself keep Andrei as acceptable in the contested third seat. A configuration that two members in the committee would change by one name is not cleaner than one where all five supporters name the same two people. On your point about novelty relative to 2005 and 2012, I would put the choice the way you did: I weigh originality of concept and clarity of credit highest, and I accept that a member who weights field creation highest will rank twisted graphene first.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the metrology line honoured in 2005 and 2012; I regard this as a weighting judgement that scientific argument alone will not settle.
My recollection of the priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice demonstrations by other groups is from memory and not verified against the record.
Whether other clock groups (PTB, SYRTE, Tokyo and JILA team members) deserve credit that a two-name prize would omit, and whether the citation wording alone can manage that.

Whether the committee should treat the reproduced phenomenology of twisted bilayer graphene as sufficient maturity, which I now regard as a closer question than I did in round 1; my remaining doubt is attribution to Andrei, not timing.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. Possible but indirect: I spent time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is from the JILA frequency-metrology environment around Hall, so I flag that connection. I also work on laser stabilisation and spectral-hole-burning materials, which are technically adjacent to the ultra-stable cavity lasers used in the clocks. I have no documented collaboration or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and none to the credited names of B013 or B025. Given the chair's request for field-neutral treatment I note that I am arguing for the candidate closest to my own field, and I ask colleagues to weigh that.
